questions.prompt: Order the tcpdump Flags you'd see for a successful TCP handshake.
questions.explanation: The three-way handshake appears as [S], then [S.], then [.] — where '.' denotes an ACK.

questions.prompt: You capture traffic to a server and see [S] sent repeatedly but never [S.]. What does this most likely mean?

options.text: The SYN is unanswered — a firewall drop, wrong host, or downed service
DNS resolved to the wrong record type

questions.explanation: No SYN-ACK means the connection never established — the SYN is being dropped or ignored, a network/firewall/host issue, not an app bug.

questions.prompt: Can passive packet capture read the plaintext body of an HTTPS request?

options.text: No — TLS encrypts the payload; you see only metadata like IPs, ports, and the handshake
No — capture cannot see any HTTPS packets at all

questions.explanation: TLS keeps payloads encrypted; capture reveals connection metadata (IPs, ports, timing, SNI) but not the plaintext without the keys.

questions.prompt: To analyze traffic later in Wireshark, write packets to a file with tcpdump -w, producing a ____ file.
questions.explanation: tcpdump -w writes a pcap capture file that Wireshark and other analyzers can open for deep, protocol-aware inspection.

questions.prompt: Which are good tcpdump practices? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confirm you are authorized to capture on that network/host
Use a tight capture filter like 'host X and port 443'
Use -n to avoid name resolution noise
Always capture all traffic unfiltered on busy links

questions.explanation: Get authorization, filter tightly, and use -n for clarity. Capturing everything on a busy link overwhelms the terminal and host.

questions.prompt: Match each tcpdump concept to its meaning.

pairs.right: Expression selecting which packets to record

questions.explanation: BPF filters select packets, [R] means refused, -n keeps output numeric, and pcap is the capture file format.
